summary: Describes an EPP extension for stronger login security. It allows longer passwords and passphrases than the basic schema, and supports more password management features.

eli5.summary: Domain registrars log in with passwords that were limited. This lets them use longer, safer ones.

questions: how to use longer passwords in epp
what is the epp login security extension
what are epp login security events
subtitle: An EPP extension that lifts the 16-character password cap and lets servers send security warnings at login.

tldr.problem: The EPP login command limits passwords to 16 characters and offers no way for a server to warn a client about expiring passwords, weak TLS settings or other login problems.
tldr.mechanism: A login extension carries a longer password in its own element, selected by the placeholder value [LOGIN-SECURITY], plus optional client user-agent details. The server can answer with a list of security events.
tldr.outcome: Registries and registrars can use passphrases of any length the server allows and learn about problems such as expiring certificates before they turn into failures.

today: RFC 8807 is a Proposed Standard from August 2020, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it. It extends the core EPP login defined in RFC 5730.

sections.title: Why the EPP Login Needed an Extension
sections.content:
The Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP, RFC 5730) authenticates a client with a user identifier and a password. The password field has a maximum length of 16 characters, which makes it hard to apply stronger password policies with higher entropy.

This document defines an extension to the EPP login command that supports passwords or passphrases longer than 16 characters. It also lets the server return a list of security events in the login response. The supported events cover password expiry, client certificate expiry, an insecure cipher, an insecure TLS protocol, a new password that fails the complexity rules, a login security statistical warning, and a custom event.
sections.eli5: The old password box was too small, like a lock that only takes a short key. This adds a bigger lock and a way for the door to tell you when something needs fixing.

sections.title: The Long Password Placeholder
sections.content:
The extension does not replace the standard pw and newPW elements. Instead, a client sets the standard element to the predefined string [LOGIN-SECURITY]. That tells the server to read the password from the extension's loginSec:pw element (or, for the new password, loginSec:newPW) instead. Servers MUST support this placeholder, and MUST NOT let a client set a password to the literal value [LOGIN-SECURITY].

The two can be mixed. A client can log in with the normal short pw and still set a long new password through loginSec:newPW.

Extension passwords are case sensitive and at least 6 characters long, with the maximum left to server policy. Leading and trailing whitespace is removed, and each run of internal whitespace (tab, linefeed, carriage return or space) becomes a single space. The RFC recommends printable ASCII characters with high entropy, such as 128 bits. For non-ASCII passwords it recommends the OpaqueString profile of PRECIS from RFC 8265 in the absence of other considerations.
sections.eli5: You write 'look in the other box' on the small form, and put your long password in the other box. The server reads the other box and ignores the note.

sections.title: The Login Command Extension
sections.content:
A loginSec:loginSec element is sent in the extension part of the EPP login command. It MUST contain at least one of three optional children: userAgent, pw and newPW. The client names the extension in the svcExtension list of the login, using the namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:epp:loginSec-1.0.

The userAgent element describes the client system so the server can spot security constraints, such as deprecating or removing TLS cipher suites or protocols. It holds at least one of app (for example EPP SDK 1.0.0), tech (for example Vendor Java 11.0.6) and os (for example x86_64 Mac OS X 10.15.2). The RFC gives ABNF patterns for each, built from names and versions separated by spaces.

The user-agent data describes a system-to-system interface. It MUST NOT allow tracking of individual users or classes of users.
sections.eli5: The client can also hand over a name tag saying what software it is. That helps the server give advice, for example 'that old setup is going out of date'.

sections.title: Security Events in the Login Response
sections.content:
After a login, successful or failed, the server MUST include the extension in its response when two things are true: the client asked for the extension, and the server found at least one login security event. The response carries a loginSec:loginSecData element holding one or more loginSec:event elements. The text of each event is a free-form description with an optional language.

Each event has a REQUIRED type:

  • password: a password that will expire or has expired; exDate MUST be set.
  • certificate: a client certificate that will expire; exDate MUST be set.
  • cipher: an insecure or deprecated TLS cipher suite; name MUST be set.
  • tlsProtocol: an insecure or deprecated TLS protocol; name MUST be set.
  • newPW: the new password fails the server's complexity requirements.
  • stat: a statistical warning, such as many failed logins; name MUST be set to the statistic's subtype.
  • custom: a server-defined event; name MUST be set.

The other attributes are level (REQUIRED, either warning for something that needs action or error for something needing immediate action), exDate (when a warning has or will become an error), value (what caused the event, such as the negotiated cipher), duration (the period a statistic covers, ending when the login arrived) and lang (default en). Dates and times MUST be UTC in the extended form with upper case T and Z.
sections.eli5: The server can hand back a list of sticky notes: 'your password runs out next week', 'your connection uses an old lock', 'someone tried to guess your password 100 times'. Each note says whether it is a warning or an emergency.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC shows three login commands. In the first, the client sends [LOGIN-SECURITY] as pw and the real long password in loginSec:pw, together with a userAgent. In the second, both pw and newPW are replaced this way. In the third, the normal short pw is kept and only the new password goes through loginSec:newPW.

The response examples include a successful login (result code 1000) warning that the password expires in a week, and a failed login (result code 2200, authentication error) reporting an expired password together with a new password that does not meet complexity requirements. A third example returns six events at once: password, certificate, cipher, TLS protocol, a failedLogins statistic with value 100 and duration P1D, and a custom event.
sections.eli5: The examples show a short sign-in form pointing to the long password, and then different sticky-note lists coming back for good and bad logins.

sections.title: Versioning and Migration
sections.content:
Servers SHOULD help clients move to newer versions of the extension, which are expected to use an XML namespace with a higher version number. For a temporary migration period, up to server policy, servers SHOULD support older versions in parallel and let clients pick through the svcExtension element of the login.

If a client asks for several versions at login, the server SHOULD answer commands that carry no extension elements using only the newest requested version. For commands that do carry extension elements, it SHOULD answer only in the versions present in the command. The extension's namespace is registered as urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:epp:loginSec-1.0 and its schema as urn:ietf:params:xml:schema:epp:loginSec-1.0, and the extension is listed in the EPP extension registry of RFC 7451 with status Active.
sections.eli5: When a new edition comes out, the server keeps the old edition around for a while so nobody gets locked out suddenly.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The server SHOULD enforce minimum and maximum password lengths suited to its environment. The RFC points to Section 5 of NIST Special Publication 800-63B as an example of guidance. Clients SHOULD NOT weaken a new password by shortening the current one: a client with a 20-character password set through the extension should not use the plain login to set a new password of 16 characters or fewer.

Returning security events to unauthenticated users needs care, because it may reveal information to potential attackers. Servers must weigh those security and privacy issues before deciding what to send.
sections.eli5: Do not swap a long key for a short one, and do not tell strangers too much about why a login failed.
